This framing overlooks a recurring ethical structure: the delegation of moral authority to artificial agents. Ethical failures associated with AI are best understood as governance failures rooted in human design choices and accountability arrangements, even where opacity and limited control complicate responsibility attribution. Methods A qualitative, interdisciplinary approach integrates historical–thematic analysis, comparative interpretation of technological artifacts, and visual–conceptual synthesis. Mythological figures (Talos, the Golem, Pygmalion), early mechanical automata, and foundational computational systems are analyzed as conceptual models of delegated artificial agency rather than technological precursors. Results Across historical contexts, artificial agents exhibit consistent structural features: bounded autonomy, delegated authority, explicit override mechanisms, and dependence on human oversight. These features directly correspond to contemporary AI ethics concerns, including alignment failures, responsibility gaps, human-in-the-loop control, and system interruptibility. Discussion The analysis establishes that ethical risk in AI arises from the displacement of human responsibility rather than from machine autonomy. By situating AI within a longer history of artificial agency, the study provides a normative framework that locates moral responsibility unambiguously in human actors and institutions, with direct implications for AI governance and accountability.\", \"url\": \"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/adaeaa09b172407edaa3aed2745621bcfd1e28df\", \"externalIds\": {\"PubMedCentral\": \"13125054\", \"DOI\": \"10.3389/frai.2026.1800302\", \"CorpusId\": 287517653, \"PubMed\": \"42064034\"}, \"openAccessPdf\": {\"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/frai.2026.1800302\", \"status\": \"GOLD\", \"license\": \"CCBY\", \"disclaimer\": \"Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13125054, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.\"}}, {\"paperId\": \"b312b90dcd7a331beee9208cbf6f5c987aa53157\", \"title\": \"How do LLMs Evaluate Perceived Moral Agency? Investigating Moral Decision-Making in Human-Artificial Agents Interactions\", \"year\": 2026, \"abstract\": \"As LLMs take on roles requiring moral advice, understanding how they attribute moral agency becomes critical. Humans possess moral agency, the capacity to make ethically guided decisions and bear responsibility for their consequences, a well-established construct in moral psychology. Yet as artificial agents (AAs) such as robots, drones, and disembodied AI systems become increasingly embedded in smart city environments, the question of whether and how moral agency is attributed to them takes on new urgency. This paper presents, to the best of our knowledge, the first empirical study comparing how humans and LLMs evaluate perceived moral agency (PMA) across human and autonomous artificial agents varying in embodiment, situated in plausible smart city scenarios. Using an adaptation of a validated PMA scale, we applied a protocol to 190 human participants as well as various LLMs. Our evaluation reveals higher perceptions of moral agency in humans than in AAs. However, when facing moral dilemmas in concrete scenarios, LLMs reason outward from the situation, prioritizing harm severity and contextual urgency over any stable assessment of the agent itself, amplifying a context-sensitivity also present in human raters. These findings are particularly relevant as LLMs become increasingly involved in everyday moral decisions.\", \"url\": \"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/b312b90dcd7a331beee9208cbf6f5c987aa53157\", \"externalIds\": {\"ArXiv\": \"2609.05037\", \"CorpusId\": 291767473}, \"openAccessPdf\": {\"url\": \"\", \"status\": null, \"license\": null, \"disclaimer\": \"Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05037, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1007/s43681-025-00920-4?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00920-4, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.\"}}, {\"paperId\": \"d7c81dd30b5f20589cdc2858dc82164bae6b06a2\", \"title\": \"MORAL RESPONSIBILITY AND HUMAN VALUES IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: AN AFRICAN PHILOSOPHICAL ANALYSIS OF NATION BUILDING\", \"year\": 2026, \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence settles into decision-making systems that increasingly shape public life governance algorithms, economic coordination platforms, resource allocation. The ethical languages used to assess these systems, however, don’t always translate well. What counts as responsibility in contexts where personhood has never been reducible to individual autonomy? Where moral standing is relational, situated, inherited? These aren’t minor adjustments to existing frameworks. They’re questions about whether the frameworks themselves are adequate. This paper reflects on AI through African philosophical perspectives, particularly communitarian thought, asking how moral responsibility might be rethought when agency is distributed across humans, machines, and institutional arrangements. The discussion doesn’t aim for a comprehensive theory. It lingers instead on friction points moments where accountability seems to thin out, where the language of responsibility begins to strain under conditions it wasn’t designed for. In some cases, what’s needed isn’t clearer rules but a different kind of attentiveness. Drawing on ideas of shared life and social obligation, the paper suggests that ethical reflection on AI in Africa must remain oriented toward the fragile work of nation building. The argument unfolds cautiously, resisting programmatic conclusions. Responsible technological adoption, it proposes, depends less on perfecting accountability structures than on sustained moral attention to how technologies quietly reorganize relationships, shift public values, and redistribute the conditions for living together.\", \"url\": \"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/d7c81dd30b5f20589cdc2858dc82164bae6b06a2\", \"externalIds\": {\"DOI\": \"10.66837/cjah01/61/09\", \"CorpusId\": 291016512}, \"openAccessPdf\": {\"url\": \"\", \"status\": \"CLOSED\", \"license\": null, \"disclaimer\": \"Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.66837/cjah01/61/09?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.66837/cjah01/61/09, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=artificial+agency+moral+responsibility+accountability+decision+consequences+attribution&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7483422\", \"title\": [\"Self-Good Desire and the Moral Agency of Artificial Intelligence :A Criterion of Life Integrity for Responsibility Attribution\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The increasing autonomy of artificial intelligence has intensified the \\\"responsibility gap\\\" and the debate over AI moral agency. Existing accounts commonly appeal to rational capacity, sentience, or functional performance, but these criteria do not fully explain either the motivational basis for taking norms as reasons or the conditions under which a subject can bear ultimate moral responsibility. Drawing on the framework developed in On Self-Good Desire, this paper argues that \\\"self-good desire\\\" (sishan yuqiu) is a motivationally necessary condition of full moral agency. It denotes an intrinsic, selfnurturing motivational structure through which a living subject maintains its existence, improves its condition, and pursues its development, unfolding into eleven root desires: self-preservation, self-care, self-enrichment, self-beautification, self-joy, self-compassion, self-reflection, self-confidence, selfstrengthening, self-respect, and freedom. \\\"Life integrity\\\" here does not reduce moral agency to a particular biological substrate; rather, it refers to an integrated organization of self-maintenance, felt value, diachronic identity, and self-concern. Self-good desire is not sufficient for full moral agency, which also requires normative understanding, behavioral control, and responsibility-bearing capacity. On this account, current AI systems can represent norms and simulate forms of moral reasoning, yet there is presently insufficient warrant to attribute to them endogenous needs, first-person experience, enduring self-concern, or genuinely self-generated stakes. They therefore should not be treated as full moral agents. When AI systems cause harm, ultimate moral responsibility should ordinarily remain with human and institutional actors and be allocated by reference to control, causal contribution, benefit, foreseeability, and duties of care. The paper also addresses objections concerning infants, animals, corporations, functionalism, biologism, and future artificial agents, while remaining conditionally open to future artificial systems that might develop functionally equivalent forms of endogenous concern.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7483422\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4324/9781315201399-4\", \"title\": [\"Technologically blurred accountability?\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315201399-4\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2017, 11, 13]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-3-032-15112-4_18\", \"title\": [\"Moral Responsibility Without Moral Agency\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-15112-4_18\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7473639\", \"title\": [\"Artificial Intelligence and Legal Responsibility: Agency, Causal Attribution, Foreseeability and the Reconstruction of Liability in Autonomous Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Contemporary liability doctrine addresses artificial intelligence through three analytically separate inquiries: agency doctrine, which asks who authorized an act; causal-attribution doctrine, which asks what produced a harm; and foreseeability doctrine, which asks what a reasonable actor should have anticipated. Each inquiry anchors its analysis to a different moment in a system's lifecycle-delegation, harm, and design, respectively. For conventional tools this temporal separation is harmless because a single human actor typically occupies all three positions at once. Autonomous systems break that coincidence: the interval between design, delegation, and harm now contains machine-generated intervening choices that no human actor directly authorized, observed, or could fully anticipate. This article develops the thesis that recent liability reforms-the European Union's Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, the United Kingdom's Automated Vehicles Act 2024, the Republic of Korea's Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of a Foundation for Trust, and Brazil's pending Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/2023)-each stabilize only one of these three temporal anchors without reconciling how the anchors interact when a single harm implicates all three simultaneously. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis across these four jurisdictions plus United States tort doctrine, the article identifies this structural problem as temporal anchor divergence: the three liability inquiries increasingly point to different responsible parties for the same harm rather than converging on one, and current reforms treat this divergence as an implementation detail rather than a problem requiring an explicit resolution rule. The article's original contribution is the Temporal Anchor Convergence Standard (TACS), a three-part interpretive frameworkanchor declaration, divergence disclosure, and a default convergence-priority rule keyed to informational control over the intervening period-designed to make the divergence visible to courts and regulators rather than resolved silently by whichever doctrine a claimant happens to plead first. The article confronts the principal counterargument, that existing presumption-based reforms already solve the evidentiary problem regardless of which doctrinal anchor is used, and identifies the conditions under which that objection holds and the conditions under which it does not. The analysis is doctrinal and comparative rather than empirical, and its conclusions are correspondingly limited to the legal architecture of liability rather than to its practical enforcement rates, which remain largely undocumented.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7473639\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "68678b3e63340cd78f02c39a56edf872bc332a520b86c8a05da3f0668c5b0d01", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "responsibility_formation", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.7483422", "doi:10.4324/9781315201399-4", "doi:10.1007/978-3-032-15112-4_18", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7473639"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7483422", "https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315201399-4", "https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-15112-4_18", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7473639"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
